article.overview: A cold-trap monitoring instrument is a measurement system intended to track the conditions inside a lunar cold trap, meaning a permanently shadowed region (PSR) or similar area cold enough that volatile substances such as water ice could remain stable for very long periods. Its core quantities are temperature and, in some designs, indicators of volatile presence or release. The catalogue entry names a measurement function rather than a specific piece of hardware, and no dedicated cold-trap monitor was identified in the sources reviewed for this article. The closest flown precedents are instruments on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), which identify cold traps from orbit [1][2], and two in-situ missions: the Chandrayaan-3 ChaSTE probe [9][10] and the MSOLO mass spectrometer on PRIME-1 [12]. Neither in-situ mission was reported to operate inside a permanently shadowed region.
article.description: A cold trap is a region of the Moon where temperatures stay low enough for volatile substances to remain frozen for very long periods. The best-known examples are permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles, which receive no direct sunlight. A cold-trap monitoring instrument would measure the thermal state of such a region and, depending on its design, indicators of volatile presence. The word monitoring implies repeated observation over time rather than a single survey. Thermal state is the main quantity. NASA describes the Diviner Lunar Radiometer as providing surface and subsurface temperature information that helps identify cold traps and potential ice deposits [1]. The Diviner team reports that temperatures within permanently shadowed craters can fall as low as 25 K, while temperatures on sunlit crater rims remain at about 220 K [2]. These are reported observations, and they show the temperature contrast that a cold-trap instrument would have to measure.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Stated purposes: (1) locate cold traps and characterise their temperature, the stated role of Diviner [1][2]; (2) identify volatile indicators, as NASA describes for LRO's LAMP instrument (surface ice and frost in the polar regions) and LEND (hydrogen distribution maps in the search for water ice) [1]; (3) support landing-hazard and terrain assessment, since NASA states Diviner data help identify rough terrain or rocks [1]; (4) support repeat observation and in-situ ground truth. A monitoring design adds a time dimension. ChaSTE and PRIME-1 show that in-situ temperature and volatile measurements can be made on the lunar surface [9][12], but neither is a long-term cold-trap time series.
article.operating_principle: No single operating principle is verified for a dedicated cold-trap monitor. The principles below are general to the measurement types named, and the flown examples show how each is implemented. Thermal radiometry: an infrared radiometer measures emitted thermal radiation and converts it to a temperature using calibrated models. Diviner is the flown example, a nine-channel infrared filter radiometer based on the design of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's Mars Climate Sounder [3]; its channels comprise two solar reflectance channels, three mineralogy channels near 8 µm and four thermal channels [3][4]. Contact temperature and penetration sensing: a probe pushed into the regolith carries temperature sensors along its length; ChaSTE is the flown example, with a heater mounted at its tip [9]. Neutron and mass-spectrometric sensing: LEND detects neutrons produced in the upper one to two metres of regolith, and its counts depend on the hydrogen content of the ground [8]; MSOLO is a commercial mass spectrometer that measured gases during drilling and surface operations on PRIME-1 [12].
article.scientific_importance: Cold traps are of scientific interest because they may hold water ice and other volatiles. NASA's LRO pages describe the mission as helping to identify polar resources such as water [1]. The Diviner south polar cold-trap results were published in Science in 2010 [5]. Identifying where cold traps are, and how cold they are, is the first step in assessing those deposits. Repeated monitoring could additionally show whether cold-trap temperatures and volatile signatures change with illumination or impact activity. The 2009 LCROSS impact into the permanently shadowed crater Cabeus detected water in the ejecta. A later secondary summary reports roughly 155 kg of water vapour and ice, and an estimate that about 5.6 per cent (plus or minus 2.9 per cent) of the crater's total mass is water ice [11]. No dedicated cold-trap monitoring time series was identified in the sources reviewed, so the temporal role remains a stated purpose rather than a demonstrated result.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a cold-trap monitoring instrument, and none was verified for a dedicated design. The examples below are the nearest flown precedents. Where mass or power is given, it is a launch-era or mission figure for the named instrument only. Where a value is absent, it is reported as not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Diviner Lunar Radiometer (LRO)
examples.type: Flown orbital thermal radiometer (closest orbital analogue); launched with LRO on 18 June 2009
examples.channels: Nine infrared channels: two broadband solar reflectance (0.3 to 3 µm), three mineralogy near 8 µm, four thermal from 12.5 µm to beyond 200 µm. Telescope A carries channels A1 to A6; telescope B carries B1 to B3.
examples.minimum_detectable_temperature_k: Below 30 K for channels B2 and B3
examples.mass_power_note: Launch-era figures from Spaceflight Now; not confirmed against an instrument document.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.operational_status: UCLA reports continuous operation since July 2009; current status not confirmed.
examples.band_edge_note: A search summary of the UCLA specifications page gave a far-infrared range of 25 to 500 µm; the fetched UCLA page did not state band edges. The PDS document gives beyond 200 µm. Unresolved.

examples.name: LEND (LRO)
examples.type: Flown neutron detector (indirect hydrogen indicator, not a temperature monitor)
examples.heritage: Follow-on to the HEND instrument on Mars Odyssey, with collimated detectors added for spatial resolution.
examples.neutron_sensors: Nine: four collimated high-pressure helium-3 proportional counters with cadmium-foil covers (CSETN1-4) and four external helium-3 detectors (one epithermal, three thermal).
examples.performance_goals: One PDS page gives a goal of about 100 ppm hydrogen by weight at 5 km horizontal resolution; a separate PSI context page describes a global model at 20 to 50 km resolution. These appear to describe different products and are not reconciled.
examples.mass_power_note: Launch-era figures from Spaceflight Now; not confirmed against an instrument document.

examples.name: ChaSTE (Chandrayaan-3)
examples.type: Flown in-situ thermal and penetration probe on the Vikram lander, which landed on 23 August 2023
examples.probe_form: Sharp-tipped, rod-shaped probe pushed into the regolith
examples.sensor_count_and_spacing: Not stated in the official ISRO summary. A secondary summary reports ten sensors; not confirmed.
examples.heater: Heater mounted at the probe tip; power not stated.
examples.observation_window: 16:20 to 17:17 local time at the post-hop location; sharp temperature drop after 17:00 local time
examples.regolith_properties: Cohesion rises from about 300 Pa to 1600 Pa and bulk density from about 750 to 1600 kg per cubic metre between the surface and 6.5 cm.
examples.disturbance: Re-ignition of the lander engines removed about 3 cm of loose dust and exposed denser material beneath.
examples.mass_power_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: MSOLO mass spectrometer on PRIME-1
examples.type: Flown in-situ volatile instrument; commercial off-the-shelf mass spectrometer, space-hardened for the mission
examples.mission: Intuitive Machines IM-2 (Nova-C) lander, flown with the TRIDENT drill
examples.landing: March 2025, about 400 m from the intended site near Mons Mouton
examples.operations: Planned window of about ten days; operations lasted closer to ten hours.
examples.performance: NASA reports TRIDENT and MSOLO both started and performed as expected. Early MSOLO scans are interpreted as dominated by human-origin gases (propellant vented from the spacecraft and traces of Earth water). No clear lunar volatile signal reported in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dedicated cold-trap monitor was identified, so no dimensions are given for one. Diviner's dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. A future instrument's dimensions would need to be set by its measurement requirements, its thermal and mechanical mounting to the ground, and its host's interfaces.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only mass figures verified in this article are launch-era values: Diviner 11.0 kg and LEND 25.8 kg, from a Spaceflight Now article [6]. The same article gives LRO spacecraft total launch mass as 1,916 kg. These are not specifications for a cold-trap monitor.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Diviner average power 24.7 W and LEND average power 11.6 W, from a launch-era article [6]. A monitor placed inside a permanently shadowed region could not rely on solar power at that location; this is an engineering inference rather than a sourced statement. Power requirements for any specific design were not verified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Cold traps are dark and very cold. Diviner reports temperatures as low as 25 K inside permanently shadowed craters, while nearby sunlit rims are about 220 K [2]. A monitor placed inside a cold trap would therefore face a large temperature contrast with its surroundings, and its own electronics would need a thermal design that keeps them within operating limits. Temperature limits and heater budgets for any specific design were not verified. Because a permanently shadowed region receives no direct sunlight, a monitor inside one could not rely on solar power at that location. This is an engineering inference rather than a sourced statement. The ChaSTE record shows steep temperature gradients and sensitivity to surface disturbance within the top few centimetres [9]. The general lunar environment, including the absence of an atmosphere and exposure to radiation and micrometeoroids, also applies, but no source-verified values were retrieved for this article.
article.limitations: Orbital remote sensing (Diviner, LAMP, LEND, Mini-RF) observes surface or near-surface properties and cannot directly measure the composition of a deep cold-trap deposit [1][2]. Temperature measurement alone does not establish that ice is present; volatile indicators are also needed [1]. An in-situ monitor requires access to a cold trap, which is difficult to reach; no verified access design was identified. Long-term monitoring depends on power, thermal control and data return, none of which was verified for a specific design. In-situ measurements at a lander site can be disturbed by the lander itself: ChaSTE recorded erosion from engine exhaust [9], and MSOLO's early data were dominated by spacecraft-origin gases [12].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A cold-trap monitor could be delivered as a surface payload, as a host-integrated experiment, or, for mapping, as an orbital instrument. The flown orbital precedent is Diviner on LRO. The flown in-situ precedents are ChaSTE on Chandrayaan-3 and the PRIME-1 payload on IM-2.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it with a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
Use a lunar lander to deliver it to the surface, or insert a spacecraft into lunar orbit.
Deploy and position the instrument, then connect its power, data and thermal interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ChaSTE was driven into the regolith by a motor on the Vikram lander [9]. PRIME-1's TRIDENT drill and MSOLO flew on the IM-2 lander, which landed about 400 m from its target [12]. A cold-trap monitor would need deployment within or next to a permanently shadowed region, which none of these precedents demonstrates.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Diviner flew on LRO, launched on 18 June 2009 [2]. ChaSTE was flown on Chandrayaan-3, landing on 23 August 2023 [9]. PRIME-1 landed on IM-2 in March 2025 [12].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted for a future cold-trap monitor. Launch-vehicle, cruise, orbit-insertion and commissioning details for LRO were not retrieved for this article. A launch-era article gives LRO a total launch mass of 1,916 kg and spacecraft power of 685 W [6]; these are spacecraft figures, not instrument specifications.

article.historical_significance: LRO's instruments, including Diviner, LAMP, LEND, LOLA and Mini-RF, are flown precedents for mapping cold traps and ice indicators from orbit [1][2]. Diviner's reported temperatures in permanently shadowed craters define the thermal conditions a cold-trap monitor would need to survive and measure [2]. The 2009 LCROSS impact into Cabeus detected water in the ejecta of a permanently shadowed crater [11]. ChaSTE, flown on Chandrayaan-3 in 2023, was described in secondary summaries as providing the first in-situ temperature profiles near the lunar south polar region [9][10]. PRIME-1 in 2025 demonstrated a commercial mass spectrometer operating on the lunar surface, with its flight volatile results still under analysis [12]. These are precedents for the measurement function, not dedicated cold-trap monitors.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: This article covers a catalogue measurement function rather than a verified hardware design. The Diviner, LEND, ChaSTE and MSOLO values quoted here are observations, instrument descriptions or mission figures from the sources listed, not design specifications for a cold-trap monitor. No mass, dimensions, power, sensitivity, lifetime or thermal tolerance is given for a dedicated cold-trap monitoring instrument, because none was verified. Temperatures reported from orbit describe surface or near-surface conditions and do not by themselves establish subsurface ice content [1][2].

data_quality_notes: Version v2 is a full rerun. The v1 files are unchanged.

Diviner mass (11.0 kg) and average power (24.7 W), and LEND mass (25.8 kg) and power (11.6 W), come from one launch-era Spaceflight Now article [6] and were not checked against an official instrument document.

Diviner far-infrared band edges conflict: PDS gives 12.5 µm to beyond 200 µm [4]; a search summary of the UCLA page gave 25 to 500 µm, but the fetched UCLA page did not state band edges [3]. Unresolved.
Diviner's Mars Climate Sounder heritage comes from search-result summaries, not a fetched page.
Diviner's current operating status was not confirmed; the UCLA page footer is dated 2023 [2].
LEND performance goals conflict or describe different products (100 ppm at 5 km per PDS; 20 to 50 km global model per PSI context). Not reconciled.

ChaSTE sensor count, spacing and insertion depth are not stated in the official ISRO summary [9]. The ApJ primary paper [10] was not read in full. Secondary sources report different erosion depths and temperatures; this article uses only the figures on the official ISRO page.
LCROSS water quantities [11] come from a secondary news summary. The Science papers were not read.
MSOLO flight data have no peer-reviewed publication in the sources reviewed; the NASA workshop presentation [12] is a summary.
LAMP, LOLA and Mini-RF roles are carried from the NASA instrument page [1] as summarised in the earlier article version and were not re-verified in this run.
Only one image was verified (NASA Photojournal PIA12088, Diviner). Reuse terms beyond the page credit were not checked. No full-resolution download was checked.
Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
